newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel draws sharp criticism on Jerusalem housing.
newsitem.headline: Israel draws sharp criticism on Jerusalem housing.

text.p: Israel, target of international criticism for approving the construction of thousands of new homes for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem, put Palestinians on notice it would brook no violent reaction to the plan.

Palestinians countered that Israel's decision on Wednesday to build 6,500 houses for Jews, with 2,500 to be put up in the first stage, threatened the fate of the peace process and the security and the stability of the Middle East as a whole.

The homes for Jews are to be built at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel, a tree-clad hill captured by the Jewish state along with the rest of East Jerusalem and the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East war

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, mounting a defence of the plan -- under which another 3,000 housing units would be built for Arabs in other areas of Jerusalem -- said on Wednesday of Palestinian warnings the decision could unleash bloodshed:
"We will not tolerate violence... If we're challenged violently we'll have to respond and we'll respond very firmly, but I hope it doesn't come to that."
Israel's key ally Washington criticised the decision, said it "further complicates an already complicated situation".
The European Union and Jordan also voiced protest.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's aide Marwan Kanafani told reporters in Gaza that Arafat was enraged by the decision, and was "worried about the fate of the peace process and the security and stability of the region."
Arafat sent urgent letters to U.S. President Bill Clinton, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, King Hussein of Jordan, and other leaders" appealing for aid in fighting the decision.
At a news conference on Wednesday, Netanyahu painted the plan as an effort by Israel to ease a shortage of housing for Arabs and Jews in the city.

Palestinians see it as an attempt to cement Israel's hold over all of Jerusalem, pre-empting "final status" talks due to be completed by 1999. Palestinians view the holy city's eastern half as the capital of a future state.
Netanyahu said the plan would promote Arab-Jewish harmony, but said it would go on even if Arab opposition were the upshot.

"We have decided that construction within the municipal boundaries of Jerusalem is something that is exempt from the Oslo (peace) accords," he said, referring to lines drawn unilaterally by Israel and not recognised internationally.

Palestinians warned the project could set off anti-Israeli violence in the West Bank and Gaza recalling clashes that erupted in September when Israel opened a new entrance to an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.
Sixty-one Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in the violence, which almost wrecked the Israel-PLO peace process.
"I'm not going to settle for the idea of periodic bouts of terror, or large scale deliberate violence. I've never heard of negotiating peace with violence or with rifles," Netanyahu said.

His adviser Dore Gold, asked if Israel might react to unrest by delaying a planned pullout from rural West Bank areas in early March, said: "If there's violence at any given time... it's obviously very hard to proceed as we have planned."
Arafat called an emergency meeting of senior PLO officials late on Wednesday, and will reconvene his leadership on Thursday in the West Bank town of Nablus, Kanafani said.
Netanyahu aide David Bar-Illan said he expected groundbreaking at the East Jerusalem site in about two weeks.
Israel's main opposition Labour party has been subdued on the issue, with some Labour figures expressing support.
In the Hague, the European Union said it deeply deplored approval of the project. Jordan Television quoted King Hussein as saying in a letter delivered by special envoy to Netanyahu:
"The decision is bound to shake the credibility of the peace process as a whole and fuel feelings of anger that will create violence and threaten the peace-building process."
Israeli security officials told the committee they felt the Palestinians would bottle their anger, at least until bulldozers began work, security sources said.

But the army was taking no chances. Army chief Amnon Shahak ordered West Bank and Gaza commanders late on Wednesday to "ready reinforcements and gear in case of escalation and unrest in the territories" and to take steps to prevent a repetition of September gun-battles with PLO forces, an army spokesman said.
